full_judgment:
"(i) Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case the Taxes Appellate Tribunal was justified in law to hold that the assessment made on 30-6-85 was not barred by limitation. 

 (iii) Whether in the facts and in the circumstances of the case even if assuming that the notice under section 34 served on 25-12-83 was a valid one whether the Taxes Appellate Tribunal was right in maintaining that the assessment made on 30-6-85 i.e. beyond one year from the date of service of such notice was not barred by limitation." 

 5. Mr Dabiruddin Ahmed, the learned Deputy Attorney-General, appearing for the department, on the other hand, submits that for the assesse applicant it was obligatory on his part to file the return for the assessment year 1981-82 by 15-9-81 but he did not file any return whereupon the DCT issued a notice under section 22(2) of the Act calling upon the assesse applicant to file a return for the said assessment year, which was not complied with by the assesse applicant and then the DCT issued a notice under section 22(4) of the Act but this time also the assesse did neither respond to the notice nor appeared before the DCT and in spite of that several opportunities were given to the assesse applicant to place his case before the DCT but for reasons best known to him he did not seize the opportunity whereupon the DCT was compelled to give up the proceedings initiated under section 22 of the Act and fell back upon section 34 of the Act and issued a notice thereunder and thus the DCT acted within his competence and jurisdiction in issuing the notice under section 34 of the Act on 6-12-83 which was served on the assesse applicant on 25-12-83. The learned Deputy Attorney-General further submits that since in response to the notice served upon him under section 34 of the Act the assesse applicant has ultimately submitted a return he thereafter cannot call in question the legality or validity of the said notice and in support of his contention he relies on the provisions as contained in section 63(3) of the Act. The learned Deputy Attorney-General further submits that the decisions relied on by Mr Noor have no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the case inasmuch as in those cases returns were filed by the assesse whereas in the instant case no return at all was filed by the assesse applicant and„ as such, the principles of law enunciated in these decisions cannot be applied to the present case. The learned Deputy Attorney-General then submits that the submission of the applicant that the assessment was barred by limitation is also misconceived and contrary to the provision of law inasmuch as section 34(1)(a) do not provide for any time limit and, as such, the provisions as laid down in section 34(2) proviso (III) is not attracted because a notice in such a case could be served at any time and the assessment could also be completed at any time without any limitation whatsoever. The learned Deputy Attorney-General then submits that sub-section (IA) of section 34 clearly lays down that if the assesse fails to comply with notice under section 22(1) and 22(2), notice under section 34(1) can be issued at any time. The learned Deputy Attorney-General further submits that the provisions of sub-section (2) of section 34 prescribes period of limitation for assessment for assesses other than those who did not file their returns under section 22(1) and 22(2) and admittedly the applicant did not file his return under section 22(1) and 22(2) and as such comes within the exception of sub-section (2) for which no time limit is provided for and clause (g) of proviso (1) is not applicable to the applicant. The learned Deputy Attorney-General then submits that Clause (a) of section 34 (1A) did not fix any time limit for service of notice but there is time limit for service of notice under Clause (b) of that sub-section and therefore it follows that the completion of assessment within one year from the service of notice tinder section 34(1A) is applicable to those who fall under clause (b) of sub-section (IA) of section 3s and the applicant falls .under clause (a) of section 34(IA) of the Act and there is no time limit for service of notice under section 34 and there is also no time limit for completion of the assessment. 

 9. On a perusal of the judgment of the appellate Joint Commissioner of Taxes it appears that the AJCT took the view that with the issuance of the notice under section 22 on 12-3-82 the proceeding was initiated by the assessing authority for assessment of the income of the applicant and that was alive till 30-6-84 and the assessing authority should have completed the assessment under section 23(4) of the Act within that period but without resorting to section 23 of the Act the assessing authority resorted to section 34 and issued a further notice under section 34 of the Act and such notice, in the facts and circumstances of the case was uncalled for and without any warrant of law. The AJCT further observed that with the issuance of notice under section 22(2) on 12-3-82 calling for return, the proceedings for assessment of the applicant's income was afoot and whilst proceedings for assessment was pending and not terminated itself in final assessment and computation of total income, the assesses income cannot he said to have escaped assessment as it was open to assessing authority to assess the income at any time within 30-6-84. The AJCT further found that the assessment order passed by the Act was also barred by limitation in view of proviso (III) of sub-section (2) of section 34 of the Act inasmuch as the was served on the assesse applicant on 25-12-83 and the assessment was made on 30-6-85, well beyond the period of one year limitation and this question of limitation as it appears from the appellate order of AJCT was urged by the applicant as an additional ground which was of course accepted by the AJCT. The crux of the point decided by the AJCT is that the issuance of notice under section 34 of the Act during the pendency of the proceeding initiated by the assessing authority under section 22 of the Act is illegal, premature and without jurisdiction. 

 16. This brings us to the alternative, submission of Mr Noor. It is urged alternatively that even if it is found that the notice is a valid one, yet the assessment order is bad since barred by limitation, as the assessment was not made within the period of limitation as provided by section 34(2)(1)(g) of the Act. Mr Noor relying on proviso (III) of subsection (2) of section 34 read with sub-clause (a) of sub7 section (1A) of section 34 submitted that the DCT can issue a notice for escapement of assessment only after the expiry of period of assessment as contemplated by sub-section (2), proviso (III) of section 34 i.e. after the expiry of 30-6-1984. The learned Deputy Attorney-General on the other hand, contended that the period of limitation as contemplated in proviso (iii) of sub-section (2) of section 34 applies only in those cases which are covered by sub-clause (b) & (c) of sub-section (1A) of section 34. Since the applicant did not file any return either under section 22(1) or 22(2), his case is covered by (1A) (a) of section 34 and the DCT can issue notice at any time and there is no time limit for making the assessment. We do not find any substance in the submission of the learned Deputy Attorney-General because this would lead to an absurd proposition. If his contention is accepted the DCT can issue a notice at any time on the expiration of the assessment year and in that case the DCT will have a long rope. He after issuance of a notice under section 22(2) may not complete the assessment pursuant to section 23 and fall back on section 34 and thereby the mandatory provisions of section 23 shall be flouted. The DCT without discharging his legal duty, as cast upon him by section 23, may resort to the residuary provision i.e. section 34 which could never have been the intention of the legislature.
